questions.q: What does 'conditional heteroskedasticity' mean in the context of ARCH/GARCH models?
options: The model only works on seasonal data
The mean of the series changes conditional on the variance
The series has no autocorrelation
The variance, conditional on past information, changes over time rather than staying constant
questions.explain: Conditional heteroskedasticity refers to variance that is not constant but instead depends on (is conditional on) past information — exactly the behavior ordinary ARMA models assume away, and that ARCH/GARCH are built to capture.

questions.q: In an ARCH(q) model, what determines today's conditional variance?
options: A weighted sum of the past q squared shocks (residuals)
Only the GARCH beta parameter
The current day's return directly, without any squaring
Today's conditional variance depends only on the long-run unconditional variance
questions.explain: ARCH(q) defines conditional variance as omega plus a weighted sum of the previous q squared error terms, so a large recent shock directly raises today's expected variance.

questions.q: For a GARCH(1,1) model with alpha=0.08 and beta=0.90, what does this combination imply?
options: The process is stationary only if omega is negative
The process is stationary, and volatility is highly persistent since beta is large
The process is non-stationary because alpha + beta < 1
Alpha and beta must always sum to exactly 1
questions.explain: alpha + beta = 0.98 < 1, which satisfies the GARCH(1,1) stationarity condition. The large beta (0.90) indicates that volatility shocks are highly persistent — most of yesterday's variance carries forward into today.

questions.q: Why does GARCH(1,1) often outperform an ARCH(q) model with a large q in practice?
options: GARCH cannot be estimated with maximum likelihood, so it is always preferred for computational reasons
GARCH does not require any stationarity condition
GARCH adds a lagged conditional-variance term, letting one or two lags capture dynamics that ARCH might need many lags to approximate
ARCH models can never satisfy omega > 0
questions.explain: By including a lagged variance term (beta * sigma_(t-1)^2), GARCH captures persistent volatility dynamics far more efficiently than ARCH, which can only use lagged squared shocks and often needs a large q to fit comparably well.

questions.q: When calling `arch_model(returns, vol='Garch', p=1, q=1)` from Python's arch package, what do p and q represent?
options: p and q are both ignored when vol='Garch' is specified
p is the number of lagged conditional-variance (GARCH) terms, and q is the number of lagged squared-residual (ARCH) terms
p is the forecast horizon and q is the confidence level
p is the ARIMA differencing order and q is the MA order, same as statsmodels
questions.explain: In the arch package's convention, p is the GARCH lag order (lagged variance terms) and q is the ARCH lag order (lagged squared shocks) — notably the reverse of how p and q are used in ARIMA(p, d, q), a common source of confusion.
